newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget deal full of tax breaks for farmers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget deal full of tax breaks for farmers.

text.p: Life and death on the family farm will mean less of a financial burden if the proposed balanced budget deal becomes law, Republican senators said Wednesday.

Sprinkled throughout the pact reached this week with the Clinton administration are a number of tax changes that will make it easier for family farmers to leave land and other assets to their children, the senators said.
Farmers will also be able to deduct the full cost of their health insurance premiums sooner than current law allows and reduce their tax load by averaging income over three years.
"We were losing family farmers with the death tax," Representative Sam Brownback, a Kansas Republican, said at a news conference to highlight the "farm-friendly provisions" of the deal.
"Now, we'll be able to see most family farmers keep the farm from one generation to the next," he said.

Under the agreement, which Congress is expected to approve before it recesses this week, the estate tax exemption for family farms and small businesses is increased to $1.3 million in 1998, from $600,000 currently.
For the rest of the population, the estate tax exemption increases to $1.0 million over 10 years.
The different treatment reflects a "a big disparity in the way estate taxes affect farmers compared to Joe Citizen," said Pat Wolff, an American Farm Bureau Federation tax specialist.

While estate taxes are levied on only about 1 percent of the general population after death, they hit about 12 percent of commercial farmers. That's because "farmers own a lot of assets to make a living," Wolff said.
To pay the estate taxes, survivors are often forced to sell large portions of land. That often makes the remaining farm a much less viable economic unit, she said.
The budget package also provides relief by cutting the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent, from 28 percent, for investments held at least 18 months.
In addition, gains on assets purchased after 2000 and held for at least five years will be taxed at only 18 percent.
The precise details of the tax legislation are still being written, but the Republican senators said the budget deal also includes the following tax provisions:

--Allowing farmers to average their income over three years for tax purposes. This restores a provision eliminated in 1986. This provision will expire in either 1999 or 2000, depending on the final version on the bill, but the Repubican senators said they would fight for an extension.

--Accelerating the phase-in of a higher health insurance deduction for self-employed farmers and other businessmen. Currently, the deduction for farmers is scheduled to rise to 80 percent by 2006, from 40 percent now. The budget bill would increase the deduction to 100 percent "by early in the 21st century," said Sen. Conrad Burns, a Montana Republican.
--Clarifying that farmers can use deferred contracts to sell grain for delivery in the following year and not be subject to taxes on those sales in the current year.
--Maintaining the current federal excise tax exemption on ethanol until 2000, when it is currently set to expire.
